title: Bit manipulation
summary: Treat a number as a row of 1s and 0s, and use AND, OR, XOR and shifts for compact flags and a few clever tricks.

sections.heading: Numbers are rows of bits
body: Every whole number is stored in binary. 13 is `1101`: 8 + 4 + 0 + 1. Each position is worth double the one to its right.

sections.heading: AND, OR, XOR and shifts
body: These operators work on every bit position separately:
- `a << n` shifts left, multiplying by 2ⁿ; `a >> n` shifts right, dividing by 2ⁿ and rounding down.

javascript.code:
const a = 0b1100
const b = 0b1010
console.log(a & b, a | b, a ^ b)
console.log(1 << 3, 20 >> 2)

sections.heading: Flags packed into one number
body: Each bit can be an on/off switch. Give each option its own bit, turn it on with `|`, test it with `&`, and turn it off with `& ~`.

In JavaScript, always put brackets around the `&` part: `===` and `!==` are applied first, so `perms & WRITE !== 0` means `perms & (WRITE !== 0)`. The last JavaScript line below shows the wrong answer that gives. Python applies `&` first, so it does not have this trap.

javascript.code:
const READ = 1
const WRITE = 2
const DELETE = 4

let perms = READ | WRITE
console.log((perms & WRITE) !== 0, (perms & DELETE) !== 0)
perms &= ~WRITE
console.log((perms & WRITE) !== 0, perms)
console.log(perms & WRITE !== 0)

python.code:
READ = 1
WRITE = 2
DELETE = 4

perms = READ | WRITE
print(perms & WRITE != 0, perms & DELETE != 0)
perms &= ~WRITE
print((perms & WRITE) != 0, perms)

sections.heading: Two classic tricks
body: - A power of two has exactly one 1 bit, and subtracting 1 flips everything below it, so `n & (n - 1)` is 0 only for powers of two.
- `x ^ x` is 0 and `x ^ 0` is `x`. XOR every number in a list where all values come in pairs except one, and the pairs cancel out, leaving the odd one.

javascript.code:
const isPowerOfTwo = (n) => n > 0 && (n & (n - 1)) === 0
console.log(isPowerOfTwo(64), isPowerOfTwo(48))

const nums = [4, 7, 2, 7, 4]
console.log(nums.reduce((acc, n) => acc ^ n, 0))

typescript.code:
const isPowerOfTwo = (n: number): boolean => n > 0 && (n & (n - 1)) === 0
console.log(isPowerOfTwo(64), isPowerOfTwo(48))

const nums = [4, 7, 2, 7, 4]
console.log(nums.reduce((acc, n) => acc ^ n, 0))

python.code:
from functools import reduce
from operator import xor

def is_power_of_two(n):
    return n > 0 and (n & (n - 1)) == 0

print(is_power_of_two(64), is_power_of_two(48))
print(reduce(xor, [4, 7, 2, 7, 4], 0))

mistakes: Leaving out brackets in JavaScript: `n & 1 === 0` means `n & (1 === 0)`. Write `(n & 1) === 0`.
In JavaScript, bitwise operators work on 32-bit integers, so numbers above about 2 billion get mangled.
